question.:question/problem:
![](images/ca/caeed93f57e554d6bf79b8915935261abb39c6fe54cc6d7d349ff60502a96053.png)

Which of the graphs above correspond to an invertible function?

Select all that apply.

Graph positions: **I.** upper left; **II.** upper right; **III.** lower left; **IV.** lower right.
question.:question/worked-solution: Graph I is strictly increasing. Graph II has a local minimum and maximum, graph III first decreases to a visible local minimum and then increases, and graph IV is a downward parabola. Thus II, III, and IV fail the horizontal line test; only I is invertible.

knowledge_point.title: Identifying an Invertible Function From Its Graph

question.:question/problem:
![](images/89/89b0be0ca7ae1a6e76d32bfc669d6f554deaaad2055b2875e3f6a49821043205.png)

Which of the graphs above correspond to an invertible function?

Select all that apply.
question.:question/worked-solution:
A function is invertible if and only if it's a one-to-one function. To determine which of the functions are one-to-one, we use the horizontal line test.

![](images/cf/cfb095836b7498c91a5cbd9d2cb694715a0d89a12a5e6ea5ff417342c4bde798.png)

From the above, we see that:

- For graph III, any horizontal line will intersect the curve at most once, no matter where we draw the line. Therefore, graph III shows a one-to-one function. As a result, this function is invertible.

- For graphs I, II, and IV, some horizontal lines intersect the curve more than once. These are not one-to-one functions. As a result, they are not invertible.
